title: ForensicConcept: Transferable Forensic Concepts for AIGI Detection
claim: Forensic evidence in detectors is diffuse yet forms recurring concepts, unlike semantic classifiers that concentrate on object parts.
layout: 2 stacked panels: patch-grid mosaic on top, 2x4 attribution heatmap grid below
description: The figure has two stacked parts. The top part is a 2x4 grid of patch mosaics, one per generator (ADM, BigGAN, GLIDE, Midjourney, SD1.4, SD1.5, VQDM, WuKong). Each mosaic is a 5x5 grid of small image patches. Each row shows one recurring concept: white fur, dark eyes, collars and accessories, textured fur or scales, and human faces. These are the patches nearest to the concept centers. The bottom part is a 2x4 grid of attribution heatmaps over cat and dog photos. Columns are grouped under 'Nature' and 'AI'. Rows are labeled 'AIGI' for the AI-image detector and 'CatDog' for the semantic classifier. Blue-to-red heat overlays show that the AIGI detector's attention is scattered in small dots across the image. The CatDog classifier's attention is concentrated on faces and object parts. The eye goes first to the colorful patch mosaics.
caption: Forensic evidence is diffuse yet conceptualizable. Top: Dataset-specific forensic codebooks (DINOv3 with injected AIGI prior); patches nearest to concept centers reveal recurring lowlevel patterns across generators. Bottom: Attribution maps show a mismatch: an AIGI detector attends to diffuse cues, while a semantic classifier (cat vs. dog) focuses on object parts.
abstract: AI-generated image detectors achieve high accuracy on in-distribution data but often fail on unseen generators. A key obstacle to understanding this failure is the black-box nature of current detectors: they do not reveal which evidence drives their decisions. We propose ForensicConcept, a framework that extracts explicit forensic concepts from detectors and enables their transfer across backbones. Our method localizes decision-critical patches via Transformer attribution, clusters them into a compact concept codebook, and uses a concept-aligned projection to produce auditable evidence readouts. Motivated by prior studies showing that DINO representations can guide diffusion generation and exhibit concept-level correspondence with diffusion features, we introduce a generation-trace reference based on CleanDIFT diffusion features and quantify backbone-trace alignment via neighborhood-structure consistency (CKNNA). We further propose concept codebook injection to transfer diffusion-derived concepts into target backbones. Experiments on GenImage, GAN-family, and Chameleon benchmarks show consistent improvements over prior methods. We also find that CKNNA alignment predicts transfer effectiveness, providing a principled explanation for why some backbones yield more transferable forensic evidence than others.
